data.title: “It’s Outrageous,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has become one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, as demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and other advanced memory products has surged. That has led to massive share price gains, allowing Micron to reach a market capitalization of more than $1 trillion, a milestone only a dozen or so other companies have attained. Yet despite the huge run-up, the company’s earnings have grown so quickly that its valuation remains surprisingly modest.

In fact, looking at its valuation, top investor James Foord, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, says the valuation is “absurd.”

At the current share price, Micron trades at roughly 22 times trailing earnings. But that multiple looks very different when compared with the company’s latest guidance. Using the midpoint of Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter EPS guidance and annualizing it, the stock trades at less than eight times earnings. “At 20 P/E (at the time of Foord’s article), Micron already looks undervalued, and this becomes ridiculous once we annualize the coming quarter’s earnings, which will be confirmed in less than a month,” says the 5-star investor. “Micron trades at just over 7x those annualized earnings, and that tells me that the market does not believe this can continue.”

This is where Nvidia enters the picture. When Nvidia reported its fiscal second-quarter 2027 results, it said that its supply commitments had more than doubled in a single quarter, from $119 billion to $279 billion. That increase was mostly linked to memory procurement, providing evidence that demand and pricing power remain exceptionally strong.

However, Nvidia is also looking for ways to use less HBM. Its Rubin CPX accelerator uses cheaper GDDR7 memory for certain workloads, while Nvidia has also paid $20 billion to license Groq’s architecture, which relies heavily on extremely fast SRAM built directly into the processor.

That matters because HBM is one of the most profitable parts of the memory market. If Nvidia can move some of the most bandwidth-intensive AI workloads onto alternative memory architectures, HBM pricing could eventually come under pressure, hurting Micron’s margins.

Foord nevertheless believes the threat should not be overstated. SRAM currently has nowhere near enough capacity to replace HBM for the enormous AI models being developed today. The fastest workloads may run on SRAM, but the rest still needs to reside in HBM or conventional DRAM.

There is another important point: Micron is a memory manufacturer, not simply an HBM company. If AI systems shift some demand from HBM toward GDDR7 or standard DRAM, that could change Micron’s product mix rather than eliminate the underlying memory demand.

Foord will therefore be watching how much HBM Nvidia puts into its next-generation systems, whether Micron can maintain premium pricing for customized HBM4E, and how its roughly $100 billion of long-term customer agreements are renewed.

For now, the investor remains bullish. Micron’s FQ4 guide suggests “another record quarter,” and while the architectural shift could pressure HBM margins, Foord does not believe it signals the end of the AI memory boom. Nvidia’s $279 billion in supply commitments suggest the industry still expects to need enormous amounts of memory.

To this end, Foord rates MU stock a Buy. (To watch Foord’s track record, click here)

Barring one Street analyst who remains on the sidelines, all 30 other recent reviews are positive, making the consensus view a Strong Buy. At $1,554.67, the average price target points toward 12-month gains of 58%. (See Micron stock forecast)

Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) are two major players in the semiconductor industry and key rivals in the race to supply the custom chips and networking technology powering AI data centers.

Broadcom remains the much larger of the two, with a market value of roughly $1.8 trillion versus around $180 billion for Marvell, and it has a substantially broader business spanning semiconductors and infrastructure software. Marvell is a more focused semiconductor company, but it has been gaining ground in custom AI silicon and going head-to-head with Broadcom for business from the hyperscalers building their own AI chips.

Both also disappointed investors with their latest quarterly readouts. The headline numbers came in ahead of Wall Street’s estimates, but they still fell short of the sky-high expectations investors had set.

So, with both stocks now trading some distance below recent highs, investors have an opportunity to buy these AI stalwarts at a discount.

However, taking the measure of the pair, RBC’s Srini Pajjuri, an analyst ranked among the top 2% on Wall Street, thinks one stock’s case is currently stronger than the other.

Starting with Marvell, the company reported second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue and non-GAAP EPS of $2.74 billion and $0.94, respectively, ahead of the analyst’s estimates of $2.70 billion and $0.93 and consensus expectations of $2.71 billion and $0.93. Its third-quarter outlook of $3.15 billion in revenue and $1.10 in EPS also topped the analyst’s estimates of $3.0 billion and $1.05 and consensus of $3.0 billion and $1.08.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast from $11.5 billion to $12.0 billion and its fiscal 2028 outlook from $16.5 billion to $18.0 billion, implying annual growth of 45% and 50%, respectively, compared with previous expectations of 40% and 45%.

The strength was broad-based, with Marvell’s optical business benefiting from robust demand for 800G and 1.6T products and growing adoption of scale-up architectures.

Meanwhile, management expects its custom business to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027 and more than double in fiscal 2028, driven by progress with AWS Trainium and Microsoft’s MAIA XPU program. It also expects “significant acceleration” in fiscal 2029. XPU-attach programs, particularly CXL and memory expansion, are seeing strong adoption among hyperscalers as inference workloads drive demand and memory remains scarce.

Marvell provided limited details on its recently announced Google agreement, with more information expected at its October 6 analyst day. However, management reiterated its projection for more than $10 billion in custom revenue in fiscal 2029 and indicated a “significant upside bias” to previous estimates. The lack of detail might have upset investors somewhat but is not a big deal to Pajjuri. “We are not overly concerned and fully expect Google program ramps to inflect in FY29, which should drive sizable upside to current $10B+ custom revenue target,” the 5-star analyst said. “We raise estimates and believe premium valuation is justified given 45%+ topline growth, optical connectivity leadership, and strong custom XPU pipeline.”

Accordingly, Pajjuri raised his fiscal 2027 EPS estimate from $4.02 to $4.19 and his fiscal 2028 estimate from $6.01 to $6.51. He maintained an Outperform rating on the stock along with a $360 price target, a figure pointing toward 12-month returns of 72%. (To watch Pajjuri’s track record, click here)

Turning to Broadcom, its fiscal third-quarter results were also ahead of expectations, with revenue of $29.6 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $3.32, compared with the analyst’s estimates of $29.4 billion and $3.22 and the Street’s estimates of $29.2 billion and $3.22. AI revenue surged 221% year over year to $16.7 billion, exceeding the company’s previous guidance of $16 billion, while a 75% gross margin was about 150 basis points above consensus despite a higher XPU mix.

Broadcom’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $34.8 billion was broadly in line with consensus of $34.7 billion, while its $21.7 billion AI revenue forecast was slightly above the analyst’s roughly $21 billion estimate.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 AI revenue forecast to $115 billion from more than $100 billion, generally matching Pajjuri’s expectations but falling short of consensus at $123 billion. Management also pointed to strong demand from its six XPU customers and introduced a fiscal 2028 AI revenue forecast of $230 billion, driven mostly by its engagements with Anthropic and OpenAI.

Pajjuri said the extended visibility was encouraging but highlighted component supply and infrastructure readiness as “potential limiting factors.” He also noted that LLM companies have supply and financing agreements with multiple chip suppliers and cloud-service providers, creating uncertainty around silicon allocation. At roughly 18.5 times estimated 2027 earnings, Broadcom is trading at a premium of more than 30% to Nvidia on a stock-compensation-adjusted basis. “We see balanced risk/reward as solid customer engagements and multi-year visibility are outweighed by supply/LPS limitations and what we consider is a high bar for FY27/28,” he summed up.

To this end, Pajjuri rates AVGO as Sector Perform (i.e., Neutral). His $400 price target suggests shares will gain 12% over the next year.

Pajjuri’s colleagues seem to agree with half of his thesis, as the analyst consensus rates both stocks Strong Buys. data.title: Insiders Are Buying These 2 Stocks — Should You Take the Hint?
data.description:
There’s only one real trick to stock investing, but it’s a doozy. You have to figure out the right stocks to build your portfolio. There are thousands of them out there, and thousands of traders dealing in them, and their tens of millions of transactions make for a lot of noise. You need to find a signal that will cut through all of that.

This is where the insiders can make a difference for the outsiders. ‘Insider’ might sound nefarious, but it’s not – it’s just the corporate officers and board members, the senior execs whose positions make them front-row observers to company operations and opportunities and challenges. The insiders know the business, know its ins and outs, and they’ll use that knowledge when they decide to invest their own money.

Of course, you have to be aware of an important feature when insiders buy or sell their own companies’ shares. They’ll have lots of reasons to sell, from diversifying their holdings to covering taxes to liquidating for capital – but they’ll typically only have one reason to buy: they believe the shares will appreciate in value, and soon.

So, when the insiders start buying big, putting their own money down to the tune of hundreds of thousands, or even millions of dollars, investors should take notice. It’s a clear sign of confidence, from those who are in a position to know.

We have opened up the Insiders’ Hot Stocks tool at TipRanks, a data-driven tool that lets us sort through recent insider trading transactions. We’ve found two stocks that are showing recent ‘informative’ buys – let’s give them a close look, and find out if this is a hint worth following.

Dick’s Sporting Goods (DKS)

The first stock we’ll look at here, Dick’s, holds the distinction of being the US market’s largest multi-channel sporting goods retailer. The company is the dominant player in this field, offering customers varied lines of athletic equipment, apparel, footwear, and outdoor gear, including such items as high-end workout shoes, camping gear, outdoor clothing, firearms – and, of course, fishing gear and tackle, which is how the chain got its start in 1948.

Today, Dick’s is a $12 billion giant. In its fiscal year 2025, which ended on January 31, 2026, Dick’s brought in over $17 billion in total revenue. That was up some 28% year-over-year, an increase driven by the company’s acquisition of the athletic shoe retailer Foot Locker in September of 2025. The Foot Locker move gave Dick’s a much stronger position in athletic footwear, adding a major sneaker-focused retail business to its existing sporting-goods operations.

We should note here that DKS shares dropped sharply at the end of August, after the company missed badly against the expectations on its fiscal 2Q26 results. The company reported a top line of $5.59 billion, for a year-over-year gain of more than 53%, and reported a non-GAAP EPS of $3.53. But the EPS was down year-over-year from $4.38, and it missed the forecast by 23 cents per share. Revenue missed by $56.6 million. The stock fell more than 30% in the aftermath of the earnings release, and is down 36% for the past year.

That set the scene for the insider buys, with multiple purchases coming right after the drop in stock price at the end of August. Board members William Colombo, Robert Eddy, and Sandeep Mathrani all bought blocks ranging from 1,550 shares to 6,100. Mathrani laid out nearly $200K, while Eddy and Colombo paid $514K and $785.5K for their purchases. The big buy, however, came from Mark Barrenechea, also of the Board of Directors, who paid $2.222 million for 17,000 shares of DKS. Barrenechea now holds $3.82 million worth of the company’s stock.

Despite the headwinds with the Foot Locker segment, Bank of America analyst Lorraine Hutchinson believes that DKS shares will rebound going forward. She says of the company and its prospects, “We are encouraged by the strength of the Dick’s business in the face of these industry challenges, and expect 2H to represent a floor for fundamental performance at FL. With the stock now trading at 10x P/E and estimates rebased, we think continued strength at Dick’s will drive multiple expansion… The Dick’s business delivered a 4.9% comp, with core business growth even excluding the World Cup benefit. Strength remained broad-based across footwear, apparel, and hardlines, with strong trends in team sports, licensed product, running, cleats, outdoor, and emerging brands.”

Unsurprisingly, Hutchinson comes down with the bulls on Dick’s, rating the stock as a Buy, with a $200 price target that suggests a one-year upside potential of 43%. (To watch Hutchinson’s track record, click here.)

data.title: Why Tesla Stock Is Rising Today, and Why This Top Investor Says Sell Anyway
data.description:
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) stock is moving higher today as investors turn their attention to the company’s Cybercab launch event in Austin, Texas, set to take place this afternoon. The event is expected to showcase the production version of Tesla’s purpose-built autonomous vehicle, a two-seat model without a steering wheel or pedals that the company plans to use in its expanding robotaxi network.

The launch is an important moment for Tesla’s autonomous-driving ambitions, but an investor with the moniker of Deep Value Investing (DVI), who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, is not convinced it will be the game-changer some investors expect.

The investor remains cautious about the company’s robotaxi strategy and believes there are several reasons to question how quickly the business can become a meaningful financial contributor.

Promotion

200% short exposure to TSLA with TSLQ

A major concern is the gap between Tesla and Waymo when it comes to real-world autonomous driving experience. Waymo has now accumulated more than 200 million fully autonomous miles on public roads, compared with the roughly 380,000 miles of unsupervised robotaxi driving Tesla reported on its latest earnings call. DVI acknowledges that Tesla’s camera-based approach appears to have improved and does not dismiss the technology outright. However, the sheer difference in autonomous mileage highlights how much further Waymo has progressed.

Waymo is also completing more than 500,000 rides per week and has operations across roughly 11 U.S. markets. Tesla, meanwhile, has not disclosed a comparable weekly ride figure, making it difficult to measure the scale of its robotaxi operation. DVI therefore wants Tesla to provide clearer numbers at the Cybercab event, particularly on weekly rides and autonomous miles.

The Cybercab itself could give Tesla an advantage on costs. Tesla previously suggested the vehicle could cost less than $30,000 when produced at scale, while Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have historically been considerably more expensive. Its newer Ojai robotaxi appears cheaper than its Jaguar-based fleet but could still cost more than a Cybercab after hardware and import tariffs are included.

That lower cost is an important potential advantage, but the 5-star investor argues that execution remains the bigger question. Tesla’s automotive margins have deteriorated substantially from their 2021 levels, while its Services and Other segment generated a 14% gross margin in Q2. Robotaxi economics are not reported separately, so there is not yet enough evidence to show that the business is improving Tesla’s profitability.

DVI therefore reiterates a Sell rating, while acknowledging that an unexpectedly aggressive Cybercab rollout could challenge the bearish thesis. (To watch Deep Value Investing’s track record, click here)

Three of the Street’s analysts join DVI in the bear camp, but with an additional 11 Buys and 14 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Moderate Buy. However, at $377.08, the average price target implies shares are fully valued. (See Tesla stock forecast)

data.title: Billionaire Dan Loeb Said Nvidia Stock Was Undervalued. Then He Sold All His Shares. Should You Do the Same?
data.description:
Dan Loeb is one of Wall Street’s best-known activist investors. He founded Third Point in 1995 and built the firm around concentrated, event-driven investments, often taking positions in companies where he believes there is an opportunity to unlock value.

That makes his latest move involving Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) particularly interesting.

Third Point completely exited its Nvidia position during the second quarter, selling its remaining 190,000 shares. But this was actually the final stage of a much larger sell-off. At the end of 2025, Third Point owned around 2.95 million Nvidia shares. It sold roughly 2.76 million of them during Q1, leaving just 190,000 shares, before selling the remainder in Q2.

Promotion

200% short exposure to NVDA with NVDS

What makes the sale even more interesting are recent comments the billionaire made. In June, Loeb said he believed Nvidia was still undervalued despite the company’s massive $5 trillion market cap.

So why did Loeb sell? One possible explanation is profit-taking. Third Point is not necessarily a buy-and-forget investor. Loeb tends to move money around when he sees better opportunities, and the average stock among the fund’s 20 largest positions had been held for just nine months as of June 30.

That makes the Nvidia sale look less like a straightforward bet against AI and more like a decision to take money off the table and redeploy it elsewhere. Loeb also sold Broadcom and Meta at the same time as Nvidia, while dramatically increasing his Alphabet position and opening a large new position in Warner Bros. Discovery. So it could be that Nvidia had performed well, but Loeb believes he can earn better returns elsewhere.

There is, however, definitely a case to ignore Loeb’s decision. Nvidia’s latest results were exceptionally strong. Fiscal second-quarter revenue jumped 56% sequentially and 73% year-over-year to $96.2 billion, while data-center revenue reached $89 billion. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share vs. Wall Street’s $2.09 estimate.

Importantly, Nvidia expects revenue of about $108 billion in the current quarter. Analysts had been expecting roughly $104.2 billion. The company is also forecasting around 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, far above Wall Street’s previous expectations of roughly 44%.

The company remains at the center of the AI infrastructure boom, and demand for its processors continues to exceed what it can supply. Its results suggest that the huge amounts being spent on AI infrastructure are still translating into enormous revenue growth.

There are some risks to the bull case, however. Higher memory costs could put pressure on Nvidia’s margins. Its business in China remains uncertain. And the biggest technology companies are developing their own AI chips, which could eventually reduce their reliance on Nvidia.

In any case, the Street’s analysts all disagree with Loeb’s move. The stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on a unanimous 30 Buys. At $329.32, the average price target implies shares will gain 45% over the one-year time frame. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

data.title: AMD vs. Oracle: One AI Stock Is a Buy, the Other’s Future Is Cloudy, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) are both participating in the AI infrastructure boom but they play different roles. AMD supplies the CPUs and AI accelerators powering data centers and is taking on Nvidia in the market for AI chips. Its Helios rack-scale systems are designed to capture more of the accelerator opportunity. Oracle sits further down the chain, providing the cloud and data-center infrastructure needed to deploy AI computing at scale.

That gives both stocks exposure to the same powerful spending trend, but through very different business models. AMD must turn soaring accelerator demand into profitable growth while protecting margins, whereas Oracle is spending enormous sums to build the infrastructure required to fulfill its AI contracts.

Top investor Louis Gerard has been taking a closer look at both names and his analysis centers on whether those economics justify the current valuations.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Assessing AMD, the chip giant’s latest results were strong. In Q2, revenue rose 50% year-over-year to $11.54 billion, while non-GAAP EPS jumped 82% to $1.66. Data center operating income swung from a loss a year earlier to $2.1 billion. AMD expects Q3 revenue of $12.7 billion to $13.3 billion, implying about 41% YoY growth and topping the $12.5 billion consensus estimate.

The main concern for Gerard is margins. AMD guided for 56% gross margin again despite expecting revenue to rise another 13% sequentially. Gerard sees HBM4 pricing as the key issue. AMD’s MI455X uses 432GB of HBM4, giving it a capacity advantage but also exposing it to higher memory costs. If HBM4 prices rise sharply into 2027, AMD could need roughly a 9%-10% increase in rack pricing simply to maintain current margins.

The 5-star investor believes that is manageable because Nvidia is also expected to raise server prices, indicating that higher memory costs can be passed on to hyperscalers. Demand remains strong, with the Helios rack-scale AI system entering production and accelerator demand reportedly running ahead of expectations. The bigger issue is valuation: AMD trades at more than 80 times non-GAAP earnings and has a free-cash-flow yield of only about 1.1%. Yet Gerard argues that AMD looks more attractive when viewed against forward earnings, with its valuation premium to Nvidia narrowing from roughly 2x to about 1.5x.

Despite the concerns, Gerard fancies AMD’s prospects, and therefore rates the stock a Buy. (To watch Gerard’s track record, click here)

Oracle presents a different set of challenges. At the end of FQ4 (May quarter), its RPO (remaining performance obligations) reached $638 billion, up 363% YoY, but fulfilling that backlog requires enormous investment. Oracle generated negative $23.7 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2026 and spent $55.7 billion on CapEx. Debt has climbed to roughly $167 billion, alongside substantial long-term data-center lease commitments.

One positive development is that many new AI infrastructure contracts are prepaid or involve customers supplying their own hardware. This shifts some capital risk away from Oracle and improves the returns on the capital it does deploy. However, Gerard notes that customer-supplied hardware also means Oracle captures less revenue and profit per gigawatt.

Ahead of Oracle’s September 10 earnings report, Gerard is focused on what the enormous backlog actually produces. He wants evidence on AI infrastructure margins, the number of gigawatts delivered, whether the $70 billion CapEx plan remains realistic, the makeup of the RPO and the company’s free cash flow and financing needs. Any indication that Oracle needs to raise more debt would be a particularly bearish signal.

Oracle looks cheap at around 20 times non-GAAP earnings, but Gerard argues that the multiple needs context. Those earnings are being generated while the company remains dependent on external financing and continues to spend heavily on infrastructure. Meanwhile, Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) and Google have stronger balance sheets and can compete aggressively in AI computing.

Oracle’s relatively cheap valuation and shift toward prepaid and customer-supplied contracts have improved its risk profile, but how profitable its massive AI infrastructure buildout will ultimately be remains unclear.

As such, Gerard maintains a Hold rating on the stock.

The Street’s analysts see no reason to pick between the pair, rating both as Strong Buys. AMD’s $647.19 average price target offers one-year upside of 45%. ORCL shares are expected to appreciate by 69%, given the average target clocks in at $254.57. (See AMD stock forecast or ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia vs. Micron: Own One AI Stock, but Stay Away From the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) have both made the most of the AI opportunity, although they have benefited from it in different ways.

Nvidia has emerged as the dominant supplier of the GPUs and networking technology needed to power AI data centers, with hyperscalers and other customers spending heavily on its latest-generation chips. Micron, meanwhile, has benefited from the surge in demand for high-performance memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is essential for feeding AI accelerators with data. As AI models become more sophisticated and data center workloads grow, both companies are seeing their technologies become ever more critical to the AI infrastructure buildout.

NVDA’s share gains have catapulted it to the status as the world’s most valuable company, while more recently, Micron stock has delivered massive returns that have helped it join the $1 trillion+ market cap club.

Promotion

But which has better prospects moving forward? Investor Bruno Montoya Amador has been taking a look at both and thinks only one is worthy of investors’ cash right now.

Looking at chip king Nvidia, the company has continued to benefit from massive spending by hyperscalers and AI-focused cloud providers, with its latest results showing little sign of a slowdown. In Q2 FY27, revenue, gross profit, operating income, and net income climbed 106%, 113%, 124%, and 126%, respectively, compared to the year-ago period. AI infrastructure spending is also expected to reach roughly $800 billion in 2026, providing a powerful catalyst for Nvidia’s business.

The main concern is how long hyperscalers can sustain such enormous capital expenditures. Companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are developing their own AI chips, partly to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and its CUDA ecosystem. Montoya Amador sees this as a longer-term threat, particularly if custom-chip development becomes cheaper and more accessible. For now, though, Nvidia remains difficult to displace. Revenue from its hyperscale customers rose 102% YoY to $48.7 billion, while its AI cloud, industrial and enterprise business also grew rapidly.

Nvidia’s growing relationship with so-called NeoCloud providers is another area worth watching. The company has helped these businesses secure financing by committing to purchase computing capacity through take-or-pay agreements, essentially providing lenders with greater confidence in future cash flows. Montoya Amador believes the arrangement creates some risk because Nvidia can simultaneously act as an investor, seller, guarantor, and potential buyer of last resort. Still, he does not consider its $56 billion in disclosed commitments particularly alarming relative to Nvidia’s roughly $300 billion in trailing-12-month revenue. For him, the bigger issues are whether hyperscaler spending remains strong and whether those investments continue generating acceptable returns.

Overall, he rates Nvidia a Buy, while emphasizing the importance of monitoring hyperscaler capital spending, returns on investment and the growth of Nvidia’s commitments. (To watch Montoya Amador’s track record, click here)

Micron presents a different picture. The company delivered extraordinary fiscal Q3 2026 results, with revenue soaring 346% YoY and net income jumping nearly 1,400%. Yet the stock remains relatively inexpensive compared with many semiconductor peers, reflecting investors’ concerns about the highly cyclical nature of the memory market.

Micron is trying to reduce that cyclicality through new five-year SCAs (strategic customer agreements). Sixteen agreements cover roughly 20% of its DRAM volume and one-third of its NAND volume through 2030, with the company expecting about half or more of its revenue eventually to fall under these arrangements. The contracts include take-or-pay provisions and roughly $100 billion of minimum committed revenue from 14 agreements, providing Micron with much greater visibility than it historically enjoyed.

However, Montoya Amador remains skeptical. data.title: Wall Street vs. Short Sellers: 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks That Could Squeeze
data.description:
Stock investing is all about balancing risk and reward, and nowhere is that more true than in short selling. Essentially, a short seller is betting that a stock will drop in price in the near-term; he sells ‘borrowed’ shares, hoping to close his position by buying them back, to return, at a lower price than he sold – and making a profit on the difference.

The conventional wisdom on short selling is that it’s an indication of clear weakness in a stock. After all, large-scale short-selling is a literal bet that the shares will lose money. But the facts on the ground are more complex, because high-value, fundamentally sound stocks can attract short sellers. In these cases, the short sellers are not actually betting against the stock, but they are betting that the share price will correct in the near-term.

Of course, the stock could gain – and that could trigger a short squeeze. It’s a classic trap. The short seller is betting on a near-term price drop, so he can eventually buy back the shares at a lower price, close his position, and turn a profit. But if the stock gains instead, he faces mounting losses – and could be forced to close his position at a loss.

Salesforce receives a far less enthusiastic assessment. The company is coming off a much better-than-expected quarter, with investors subsequently sending shares up by almost 23% in the aftermath.

For Liani, however, the significance of the results goes beyond the headline numbers. He argues that the quarter was encouraging because it undermined the argument that AI will ultimately make Salesforce obsolete. Instead, the focus of the debate is moving away from whether AI will replace CRM platforms and toward whether Salesforce can successfully turn AI adoption into additional revenue growth. The latest results suggest that the underlying CRM business remains steady while the company’s AI initiatives “continue to gain traction.”

AI still accounts for only a modest portion of Salesforce’s business. Agentforce ARR stands at $1.5 billion compared with a $46 billion revenue base. Nevertheless, Liani acknowledges that Salesforce is making tangible progress in incorporating AI into its platform and generating revenue from it. Agentforce ARR has risen by more than 240% YoY, platform usage continues to expand, and the partnership with Anthropic adds an “important context across additional surfaces.” Another encouraging sign is that around half of Agentforce bookings came from credit refills, pointing to continued customer use and recurring engagement.

However, that is not enough to alter Liani’s bearish thesis.

Liani reiterated an Underperform (i.e., Sell) rating on an “unbalanced risk/reward setup with moderate growth levels, AI being too nascent to impact the revenue profile, and current valuation at the high-end of peers.”

Liani’s $160 price objective remains the Street’s lowest and suggests the stock is overvalued by 38%. (To watch Liani’s track record, click here)

data.title: Broadcom vs. AMD: Which AI Stock Represents the Better Opportunity? Investor Weighs In
data.description:
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) are both benefiting from the huge sums being invested in artificial intelligence, but they occupy different positions within the AI hardware market.

Broadcom is a major supplier of custom AI accelerators and networking technology, while AMD sells GPUs and CPUs and is pushing deeper into complete AI computing systems. Both companies already have significant relationships with major technology companies, making the comparison less about whether hyperscalers are embracing them and more about where each can capture the most value as AI infrastructure expands.

For investors, the key difference is the nature of that opportunity. Broadcom has built a substantial business around custom silicon, with major customers using its technology to develop chips tailored to their own AI workloads. AMD, meanwhile, is competing for a larger share of the accelerator market while also benefiting from its position in CPUs.

Investor Micah Zimmerman, who contributes to The Motley Fool, has been examining the two companies and believes their contrasting strategies create very different investment cases.

Broadcom’s strength lies in custom AI infrastructure. The company works with major tech companies including Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms to develop application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs. These chips are designed around the particular workloads and power requirements of each customer rather than being general-purpose products. That can make them more efficient for specific applications and gives hyperscalers another way to handle growing AI workloads alongside conventional GPUs.

The scale of Broadcom’s opportunity is already substantial. AI semiconductor revenue was around $8.4 billion per quarter, while its disclosed AI chip backlog stood at roughly $73 billion. Management has also pointed to a path toward more than $100 billion in AI revenue in 2027. Its networking business adds another important source of exposure because more powerful AI systems require high-speed connections between large numbers of processors. Broadcom also has established businesses in areas such as broadband and enterprise software, giving it a broader revenue base.

AMD’s opportunity is different but no less significant. The company has secured major AI commitments of its own and is using its Instinct accelerators and Helios rack systems to compete directly with Nvidia in data center AI. Its MI355X accelerator has demonstrated strong performance in some large-language-model workloads and offers more memory than Nvidia’s B200.

The challenge is that competition extends beyond the accelerator itself. Nvidia’s latest platforms combine GPUs, CPUs, networking and software into integrated systems, while CUDA and TensorRT give developers a mature software ecosystem. AMD’s ROCm platform and Helios systems therefore need to demonstrate that they can provide customers with a competitive end-to-end solution. That is a much bigger task than simply matching Nvidia on chip performance.

There is another potential advantage for AMD, however: CPUs. As AI data centers evolve towards more complex workloads, demand for server CPUs could rise alongside accelerator demand. AMD is already a major player in this market, giving it an additional avenue for growth that Broadcom does not currently have.

This leaves investors with two companies benefiting from the same broad AI spending boom but through different routes. Broadcom has considerable visibility because of its established custom-silicon and networking programs, while AMD has the opportunity to expand across both accelerators and CPUs if its products gain further traction.

In Zimmerman’s view, therefore, Broadcom represents the steadier AI investment, while AMD offers greater speculative upside. For investors, the choice ultimately comes down to whether they prefer Broadcom’s greater visibility or AMD’s higher-risk opportunity to deliver a more significant transformation. data.title: Billionaire David Tepper Dumped All His Sandisk Stock. Should You?
data.description:
David Tepper is one of Wall Street’s most closely watched billionaire investors. The founder and president of Appaloosa Management has built a reputation for making big, often contrarian bets and has generated some spectacular returns over his career, with Appaloosa delivering annualized returns of roughly 28% since its launch in 1993.

Now, one of his latest moves is raising eyebrows. Tepper has completely dumped his position in memory high-flyer Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK).

According to Appaloosa’s latest 13F filing, the hedge fund held no Sandisk shares at the end of the second quarter. That means Tepper sold his entire position after buying 281,250 shares during Q1.

Promotion

High conviction on SNDK? Try Tradr's SNXX or SNDQ

The timing here is pretty interesting. Sandisk has been one of the hottest AI-related stocks on the market, surging by almost 3,000% over the past 12 months and more than 850% during the first half of the year. The NAND flash specialist has benefited from soaring demand for memory as companies spend billions building AI infrastructure.

The company’s latest earnings show just how strong that demand has become. Sandisk reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $8.97 billion, up 372% from a year earlier and 51% from the previous quarter. Adjusted EPS came in at $39.25, compared with just 29 cents a year earlier. Even more impressive, adj. gross margin jumped to 84.6%, up from 26.2% a year earlier.

The data center business was a major part of that growth, generating around $2.98 billion in revenue, more than double the previous quarter. For the full fiscal year, SanDisk’s revenue reached $20.25 billion, up 175% from the previous year, while data center revenue increased 437%.

So Tepper was selling a stock backed by some seriously impressive numbers. But after a huge gain in just a few months, he appears to have decided that the time was right to take his winnings off the table.

While this could be seen as a bearish call on artificial intelligence, that is not the case at all. In fact, Tepper still has plenty of exposure to the AI boom.

Amazon is now Appaloosa’s largest holding, accounting for roughly 15% of its disclosed portfolio. Micron is the second-largest position at around 14.6%, while Taiwan Semiconductor represents another 10%. Tepper also owns Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, AMD, ASML and Lam Research. He even initiated a new position in Broadcom during the second quarter.

Essentially, Tepper isn’t saying AI is finished in any way. His portfolio suggests almost the opposite. Instead, he appears to be reallocating capital within the AI ecosystem, moving away from a stock that has notched massive gains, while maintaining significant exposure to companies that could benefit from continued AI spending.

Does that mean Sandisk investors should sell too?

Not according to the Street’s analysts. In fact, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 14 Buys and 2 Holds. At $2,201.56, the average price target implies shares will gain 40.5% over the coming months. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Don’t Do It,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock has bounced off the lows it plummeted in July, but the stock still sits 54% below the highs reached last September as investors continue to question the company’s heavy debt burden and enormous spending on AI data centers.

For bottom-fishers, that might seem like an opportunity to load up. Oracle is still growing rapidly, with AI-related demand driving significant revenue growth. However, top investor Paul Franke believes that would be a mistake and argues that the risks surrounding that growth are still too high.

The investor sees Oracle as a clear example of the financial challenges created by the AI infrastructure spending boom. The company has committed to massive capital expenditures to expand its cloud and data center capacity, putting increasing pressure on its free cash flow. Oracle’s trailing free cash flow yield has fallen to -5.4%, its worst level in data dating back to 1995.

Promotion

Franke argues that the wider AI industry faces a major question: how will customers ultimately pay for the trillions of dollars being invested in infrastructure?

The scale of Oracle’s spending illustrates the problem. Its planned Jupiter data center project in New Mexico is estimated to cost $165 billion over several years. That compares with Oracle’s current market cap of roughly $435 billion. Franke believes such enormous investment could become a problem if AI demand weakens or businesses reduce usage because of rising costs.

The 5-star investor is also concerned that AI infrastructure could become overbuilt if demand weakens or customers reduce their usage because of rising costs. Oracle co-founder, Chairman and CTO Larry Ellison, has essentially made AI demand a central part of the company’s future, leaving the business exposed if expectations fail to materialize.

Beyond cash flow, Franke points to Oracle’s history of underperforming broader technology investments. Over the past 10 years, Oracle’s total return has significantly trailed the Nasdaq-100, delivering a total return of around 324%, compared with 557% for the QQQ ETF. The investor also sees Oracle’s recent stock chart as particularly weak, with several technical indicators pointing to persistent selling pressure.

There are still reasons to remain optimistic. Oracle’s established software business remains valuable, while AI-related revenue could continue growing rapidly. Its forward P/E ratio is also below 20, making it cheaper than many Big Tech peers. But Franke believes that discount could reflect the additional risks surrounding Oracle’s capital spending and future cash generation.

The investor acknowledges that the shares could potentially surge ahead over the next two to three years if AI demand remains strong. Nevertheless, given the uncertain returns on its massive infrastructure investments and the stronger free-cash-flow profiles of other technology giants, Franke rates the stock a Sell.
